analysis.title: Core inflation hotter than expected, October hike back in play
key_insights: Headline CPI rose 0.6% m/m in September, the fastest pace since last April, driven by a roughly 10% increase in fuel costs.
Core CPI rose 0.33% m/m against an expectation of 0.2%. That is a 4.1% annualized pace and a 3.4% annualized pace over the past three months. Year-over-year core inflation rose to 2.6%.
The core strength was broad-based, with accelerations in shelter and core goods and a third straight month of elevated supercore inflation.
Shelter added 0.17 percentage points to the 0.33% core increase, driven by stronger rent inflation and a 2% rise in hotel prices.

Core goods prices rose 0.25% m/m (3.1% annualized), the fastest pace since January 2025. PNC says higher diesel costs are replacing tariffs as the main driver of goods inflation, and the expected moderation in 2H26 is not happening.
Supercore (core services excluding shelter) rose 0.34% m/m, versus about 0.2% common before the pandemic. It has run at a 4.5% annualized pace over three months.

PNC argues the Fed's remaining inflation problem is a demand problem, visible mainly in supercore. The Fed can look through one-time supply shocks but not a demand shock or a serial string of compounding supply shocks.
October rate hike odds rose to just over 50% after the print. PNC calls that appropriate, since a core reading rounding to 0.4% would bring an October hike into play and this print was close.
Tomorrow's PPI will help PNC estimate September core PCE, which should clarify whether the Fed hikes at the end of October. PNC expects hikes in December and again in March 2027.
